items.title: Energy can be lost in a collision; momentum cannot
items.claim: Two cars crash and lock together. Their combined kinetic energy after the collision is LESS than before (energy lost to heat, sound, deformation). But the combined momentum is exactly the same.
items.prompt: Why does momentum survive while energy doesn't?

options.text: Momentum is always conserved; energy is not

Total energy is conserved if you include heat, sound, deformation — but KINETIC energy alone is not conserved in inelastic collisions. Momentum is a vector quantity conserved by Newton's third law independent of internal energy losses
Momentum and energy are equally lost
Energy conservation only applies to electricity

items.reveal_title: Conservation laws and what they refer to
items.reveal:
Newton's third law (action and reaction) implies that internal forces in a closed system cancel pairwise. Total momentum (m1 v1 + m2 v2 + ...) does not change unless an external force acts.

This holds regardless of whether the collision is elastic (kinetic energy conserved) or inelastic (kinetic energy partly converted to heat, deformation, etc.).

Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 — proportional to v squared, so velocity SIGN doesn't matter (kinetic energy is scalar and always positive). Two equal-mass objects approaching each other with v and -v have total KE > 0 but total momentum = 0. After perfectly inelastic collision (stuck together), final velocity = 0, KE = 0. KE is lost; momentum unchanged.

Elastic collisions (snooker balls, gas molecules): both momentum and kinetic energy conserved.
Inelastic collisions (cars sticking, putty hitting wall): momentum conserved; some KE -> heat/sound/deformation.
Explosions (reverse collisions): momentum still conserved (must be balanced); KE can INCREASE (from chemical energy released).

The full energy conservation includes all forms: chemical, thermal, acoustic, electromagnetic. It's the kinetic energy alone that can vary.

The distinction is crucial for understanding everything from billiard balls to particle accelerators to car crashes to firearms.
items.why: Conservation laws are taught as universal. Different conservation laws apply to different quantities and conditions. Energy is always conserved (with all forms counted); kinetic energy alone is not.

items.title: The angles of a triangle on a globe don't add to 180 degrees
items.claim: Draw a triangle from the North Pole to the equator at 0 degrees longitude, along the equator to 90 degrees longitude, and back to the North Pole. All three angles are 90 degrees. Total: 270.
items.prompt: How can a triangle have 270 degrees?

options.text: On a curved surface, the angle sum exceeds 180 by an amount proportional to the area enclosed (spherical excess); on a sphere of radius R, sum = 180 + (area / R^2) in radians times 180/pi

items.reveal:
On a flat Euclidean plane, the angles of a triangle sum to exactly 180 degrees.

On a sphere (positive curvature), the sum is more than 180. The excess is proportional to the area: Sum - 180 = (Area / R^2) * (180/pi) for a sphere of radius R. The example triangle (pole-equator-equator-pole) covers 1/8 of the Earth's surface — area ~ 6.4 * 10^7 square km — and has excess 90 degrees.

On a hyperbolic plane (negative curvature), the sum is LESS than 180. The deficit is proportional to area.

This is the deepest test of non-Euclidean geometry: by measuring the angle sum of a triangle, you can tell what kind of space you're in.

Gauss attempted to measure the angle sum of a triangle formed by three mountain peaks (Hohenhagen, Brocken, Inselsberg) in 1820s to test whether space itself is Euclidean. He found no measurable deviation from 180, given his instruments' precision.

General relativity: mass curves space-time. Light follows geodesics through curved space-time. Two photons from a distant source, passing on either side of the Sun, converge (negative curvature in tested region's measurement frame). Detected during the 1919 solar eclipse — confirmation of Einstein.
items.why: Triangles seem to obviously sum to 180. They do on flat surfaces. Real Earth navigation, general relativity, and modern cosmology all use non-Euclidean geometry where triangle sums are observably different.

items.title: A walker who halves their distance forever still reaches the wall
items.claim: Walk halfway to a wall. Then half of what's left. Then half again. Infinitely many steps — but the total distance is finite (the original distance), and the total time (if you halve your time at each step too) is also finite. Zeno's paradox resolved.

options.text: Infinity — there are infinitely many terms
Exactly 1. Geometric series with ratio r where |r| < 1 sums to a/(1-r); here a = 1/2 and r = 1/2, so sum = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1
Depends on how many terms you take

items.reveal:
A geometric series: a + ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... For |r| < 1, the sum is a/(1-r).

Proof: let S = a + ar + ar^2 + ... Then rS = ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... = S - a. So S - rS = a, giving S = a/(1-r).

Examples:
1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = (1/2)/(1 - 1/2) = 1.
0.999... = 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... = 0.9/(1 - 0.1) = 1.
1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + ... = 1/(1 - 1/3) = 3/2.

For |r| >= 1: the series diverges. 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... grows without bound.

Zeno's paradoxes resolved: Achilles catches the tortoise in finite time because the catching-up steps form a convergent series. Modern calculus formalises 'limit' and 'sum to infinity', tools Zeno did not have.

Applications:
- Compound interest formulas (sum of payment streams).
- Mortgage/loan calculations.
- Probability of getting heads eventually in repeated coin tosses.
- Resonance in physics (geometric series of wave reflections).
- Convergence of decimal expansions, power series, Taylor expansions.

Fermat, Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy, Weierstrass — the theory of convergent series was refined over centuries. By Weierstrass's epsilon-delta formalisation (1850s), 'infinite sum equals 1' had precise rigorous meaning.

Non-convergent series: harmonic 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... diverges (slowly, but to infinity). Conditional convergence (alternating series) raises subtle issues — Riemann showed you can rearrange a conditionally convergent series to sum to any value.
items.why: Infinite tasks seem impossible. They're not: infinite quantities can sum to finite values, given the right conditions. Calculus tamed Zeno's paradoxes and made motion mathematically describable.
